text:
*Interview with Félix Monnier, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Monsieur Monnier, please sit down. You are the nephew?

FÉLIX: I am, Inspector, for my sins. Félix. Half the town thinks I'm the heir, and the other half thinks I'm the man who owes them money. I'm not sure which half is more dangerous.

MATTHEY: Tell me about dinner.

FÉLIX: My uncle was in form, which means he was unbearable. You know his custom. When the temple struck nine he had us all put our watches on the cloth. When the temple struck nine, my watch showed twenty minutes to nine. Mine is the silver one, my father's. Uncle Aurèle held it up in front of everyone like a dead fish and said it was a wreck and he would not have it in his house. He made a scene of it.

MATTHEY: Your father's watch.

FÉLIX: My father Jules died in 1889, and I have carried that watch ever since. I have never let anyone at it, not even my uncle, though he asked often enough. He thought he could put it right with a screwdriver and some oil. I told him he could have it when I was dead, which was a poor joke, and he didn't laugh.

MATTHEY: After dinner, what did you do?

FÉLIX: I went up to the library. I wanted brandy and not company, so I took the bottle and sat there alone. When the temple struck ten, my watch showed twenty to ten.

MATTHEY: Did anything happen after that?

FÉLIX: At a quarter past ten by my watch someone went quickly up the stairs past the library door. I didn't see who. The door was shut. Then at twenty-one minutes past ten by my watch someone came quickly down. Again I didn't see who, and I didn't go out to look. I'm not the sort who goes out to look.

MATTHEY: Do you know who it was?

FÉLIX: No. I have said no to that already, to myself as much as anyone, and it's still no.

MATTHEY: Go on, please, when you are ready.

FÉLIX: At eighteen minutes past ten by my watch I heard a thump on the floor right above me, in the atelier. My aunt's piano was playing downstairs when it came. Then my uncle's repeater sounded. Ten slow deep notes. I counted those. Then some doubled notes, then quick high ones that I did not count. I've heard that thing strike every New Year since I was a boy. He would stand at the bench with his hand on the slide like a priest at the elevation. He told me once it was the only honest thing in the house, because it told you the time when you asked and not before.

MATTHEY: What did the repeater mean to him?

FÉLIX: Everything. Four years of his life. He talked of nothing else. He wanted it finished for the century. You'll think I'm being sentimental, Inspector, but he was not a sentimental man, and he was proud of that.

MATTHEY: And you were in the library?

FÉLIX: Alone, yes, until Girard came in. At thirty-two minutes past ten by my watch Bastien Girard came into the library and we sat together there until the temple struck eleven. We talked about money, mostly. I owe him money. Not a great deal, though to me it is. He had wanted to buy the rights to the repeater, and he and my uncle quarrelled about the price at dinner. You'll have heard about that already.

MATTHEY: I can't tell you what I have heard, Monsieur.

FÉLIX: No, of course not. Forgive me. I talk when I'm frightened. I make jokes too, which is worse. I know how this looks. I was alone in a room directly under his bench, drinking his brandy, and I'm the heir. I can hear how that sounds in a policeman's ear.

MATTHEY: Is there anything else you want to tell me?

FÉLIX: Only that I loved him, Inspector. It's a stupid thing to say to a policeman. But nobody else is going to say it for me.
